title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.1 Goal for this week

Tell the two styles of hardware description apart: behavioral and structural
Describe sequential logic with always_ff: flip-flops, resets, registers with an enable, and counters
Know what a latch is, and write code that cannot produce one by accident
Describe combinational logic with always_comb: multiplexers and decoders
Explain the difference between = and <=, and why each block uses one of them
Assemble a design from smaller modules, and test it with a testbench

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.2 Two styles of design
There are two ways to describe a piece of hardware in SystemVerilog, and a real design uses both.
In behavioral design we describe what a block does: its outputs as a function of its inputs and, for sequential logic, of its stored state. We write that with assign and with always blocks, and leave it to the synthesis tool to pick the gates and flip-flops. In structural design we describe how a block is composed of other blocks: we create instances of smaller modules and connect their ports with wires, much as one would wire chips on a board.









Behavioral
Structural




Describes
what a block does
how it is built from other blocks


Written with
assign, always_*
module instances


Example
a register, a multiplexer
a pipeline stage



The two styles meet at the leaf cells. In the HIPV SoC that we use as a running example, the folder rtl/generic holds small, reusable cells (flopenr, mux2, mux3, adder) written in behavioral style, and the larger modules of the processor instantiate them structurally. This chapter begins with the behavioral style, because those leaf cells have to be written before they can be assembled, and ends with the structural style.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.3 The always block
The previous chapter described logic one line at a time with assign. That is enough for an adder, but awkward the moment a function needs an if or a case. For those we use an always block: a block of statements that describes how a set of outputs depends on a set of inputs.
SystemVerilog has three kinds of always block for hardware, and which one you use is dictated by what you are building:








Block
Describes
Runs when




always_comb
combinational logic
any signal it reads changes


always_ff @(posedge clk)
flip-flops
the clock edge


always_latch
latches
any of its inputs changes



The names are a promise to the tool: if the code inside does not describe the kind of hardware the block name claims, the tool reports it. Older Verilog has a single always @(...) for all three purposes, and a whole class of bugs came from getting it wrong without any warning.
Two facts about always blocks are worth keeping in mind from the start. First, every always block in a module is a separate piece of hardware that exists all the time, like an assign, so they all run concurrently and the order in which you write them does not matter. Second, the statements inside one block run in the order written, like a small program. A block is a description of hardware, not a function that gets called.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
section: 5.4 Sequential logic: describe the hardware you want
text:
5.4 Sequential logic: describe the hardware you want
Hardware description is not programming, and the habit that separates the two is this: decide on the hardware first, then write the code that describes it. If you cannot sketch the flip-flops and gates you expect, you are not ready to write the always block, and the synthesis tool will build something, but not necessarily what you meant.
So for every circuit in this chapter we follow the same four steps. First, the hardware we want. Second, its waveform, which says what the circuit must do over time and is the most precise specification there is. Third, the code that describes it. Fourth, a walk through the waveform to check that the code matches it. Learning to read waveforms is half of the work: it is also how you will debug in simulation.
A convention for all the diagrams in this chapter: the clock rises at the start of each numbered column, and input signals change in the middle of a column, after the clock has fallen. That way an input never changes at the same instant as a rising edge, and it is always clear which value the circuit sampled.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.5 The D flip-flop






Figure 5.1: A D flip-flop: q takes the value of d at each rising clock edge.



The flip-flop is the memory element of synchronous design. It has a data input d, a clock clk and an output q. At every rising edge of the clock it copies d to q, and between edges it holds that value no matter what d does (Figure 5.1).
Follow the waveform from left to right. In column 0, q is unknown (the hatched area): nothing has been stored yet. At the rising edge that starts column 1, d is 0, so q becomes 0. In the middle of column 1, d rises, and q does not react: the flip-flop is not looking. At the next rising edge, starting column 2, it samples d = 1 and q rises. The same happens in reverse when d falls in the middle of column 3: q falls only at the edge that starts column 4. A flip-flop is a circuit that looks at its input at one instant per cycle.
The code is as short as the circuit:
module dff (
    input  logic clk, d,
    output logic q
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    q <= d;
  end
endmodule
The sensitivity list @(posedge clk) names the event that makes the block run, and the block runs only then. Between clock edges nothing happens and q keeps its value: that holding is the memory. The operator is <=, the non-blocking assignment, which we explain at the end of the chapter; for now, remember that it goes with always_ff.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.6 The latch






Figure 5.2: A latch: q follows d while en is high, and holds its value while en is low.



A latch is a memory element too, but it looks at its input for a whole level, not at one instant. While the enable en is high, the latch is transparent: q follows d continuously. When en falls, the latch closes and q holds the last value (Figure 5.2).
In the waveform, en is high during columns 2 to 4. As soon as it rises, q takes the value of d, which is 1. When d falls at the start of column 4, q falls with it, because the latch is still open. en falls at the start of column 5, and from then on q stays 0: when d rises again in column 6, the latch is closed and does not notice. Compare this with the flip-flop of the previous waveform, where q could only change at a clock edge.
always_latch begin
  if (en) q <= d;
end
A latch has no clock edge, so a signal passing through it can ripple along for as long as en is high, which makes timing analysis difficult. In a synchronous design we want flip-flops everywhere, and we use a latch only on purpose. The reason to know it exists is that it is easy to build one by accident, and the section on combinational logic below shows how.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.7 Adding a reset






Figure 5.3: Synchronous reset: q clears at the next rising edge after reset rises.









Figure 5.4: Asynchronous reset: q clears the moment reset rises, without waiting for a clock edge.



A flip-flop that powers up with an unknown value is a bug waiting to happen, so registers get a reset that forces a known value. There are two ways to write it, and both clear q when reset is high. They differ in when the clear takes effect.
With a synchronous reset (Figure 5.3), reset is just another input that the flip-flop looks at on the clock edge. In the waveform d stays 1. q becomes 1 at the edge that starts column 1. reset rises in the middle of column 1 and q does not move; only at the edge starting column 2 does the flip-flop see reset high and clear. It stays cleared through the edges of columns 3 and 4 because reset is still high. reset falls in the middle of column 4, and at the edge starting column 5 the flip-flop loads d again.
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
With an asynchronous reset (Figure 5.4), the flip-flop reacts to reset itself, whatever the clock is doing. The same stimulus now clears q in the middle of column 1, the instant reset rises, not at the next edge. It stays 0 while reset is high, and after reset falls it waits for the next edge, at the start of column 5, to load d.
always_ff @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
  if (reset) q <= 1'b0;
  else       q <= d;
end
This is why reset appears in the sensitivity list next to posedge clk: the block must also run when reset rises. An asynchronous reset needs a flip-flop with a dedicated reset pin, and its release matters: if reset falls too close to a clock edge the flip-flop can misbehave, a problem we return to when we discuss synchronizers. A synchronous reset needs a running clock, but is just logic in front of the D input (or a dedicated set/reset input on an FPGA flip-flop, like the one in the slice of the previous chapter).
The HIPV SoC chooses one style for the whole design: its coding standard requires a synchronous reset throughout. That is the style we use from now on. Pick one style, use it everywhere, and know which one you picked.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.8 Registers and the enable signal






Figure 5.5: flopenr: after the reset, Q loads D only at the edges where en is high.



A single flip-flop stores one bit. A register is a group of flip-flops that load together, and in a processor most registers also need an enable: a signal that says “load a new value at this edge”, and otherwise “keep the old one”. A pipeline register that must hold its contents while the stage ahead is busy is exactly that. This is the most-instantiated cell in HIPV:
module flopenr #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic             clk, reset, en,
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Q);

  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) Q <= '0;
    else if (en) Q <= D;

endmodule
The module is the D flip-flop with a synchronous reset, plus one more condition. WIDTH is a parameter, so the same description serves for a 1-bit flag and for the 32-bit program counter. The priority is spelled out by the if/else if chain: reset wins, then enable, and if neither is active there is no assignment at all, so the register keeps its value. That “no assignment means hold” is legal inside always_ff, since a flip-flop naturally remembers; it is the opposite of the rule for always_comb, where it would build a latch.
Figure 5.5 shows the behavior. reset is high around the first edge, so at the start of column 1 Q loads 0. D carries the values A, B, C, D, changing mid-column. en is high for the edges starting columns 2, 3 and 4. At column 2 the register loads B. At column 3 D is still B, so Q stays B. At column 4 D is C, so Q loads C. Then en falls in the middle of column 4, and from the edge at column 5 on the register ignores D, even though D keeps changing: Q holds C. Figure 5.6 is what the synthesis tool builds: one flip-flop cell with clock, data, enable and synchronous reset inputs, which is what an FPGA slice flip-flop provides directly (the clock-enable and set/reset inputs of the previous chapter).






Figure 5.6: The flopenr module (8-bit by default), drawn by Yosys from the real HIPV file. $sdffe is a flip-flop with synchronous reset and enable.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
section: 5.9 Counters: two ways to write one
text:
5.9 Counters: two ways to write one
A counter is a register whose next value is its own current value plus one. Its waveform is the simplest of any sequential circuit: after the reset, the output goes up by one at every clock edge (Figure 5.7). There are two common ways to write it, and the best habit is to know both.
Way 1: everything in one always_ff. The straightforward form says, at each edge, “if reset, clear; otherwise count <= count + 1”:
module counter4 (
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       reset,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
    else       count <= count + 1;
  end
endmodule






Figure 5.7: Timing of counter4: after the reset, count increases by one at every rising edge.



At the edge starting column 1, reset is still high and count loads 0. From then on reset is low, and at each edge count takes its own value plus one: 1, 2, 3 and so on. When it reaches 15, the next + 1 wraps around to 0, because the result is truncated to 4 bits.
Way 2: next-state logic and a register. The second form splits the description in two. A combinational block computes what the next value would be, count_next, and a plain register stores it:
module counter4_next (
    input  logic       clk,
    input  logic       reset,
    output logic [3:0] count
);
  logic [3:0] count_next;

  always_comb begin
    count_next = count + 1;
  end

  always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (reset) count <= 4'b0000;
    else       count <= count_next;
  end
endmodule






Figure 5.8: Timing of counter4_next: count_next is always one ahead of count, and the register copies it at each edge.



The waveform now has one more signal (Figure 5.8). count_next is combinational, so it changes as soon as count does, and is always one higher. In column 1, count is 0 and count_next is already 1, but the register ignores it at the edge starting column 1 because reset is high. At the edge starting column 2 the register copies the 1, and so on.
Both modules synthesize to exactly the same hardware: an adder, a register with a synchronous reset, and the feedback wire (Figure 5.9).






Figure 5.9: Both counter descriptions give this circuit, drawn by Yosys: the register output feeds the output port and the adder, and reset drives the synchronous reset input.



So why bother with the second form? Because it separates two questions: what is the next value? (combinational logic) and when do we store it? (the register). For a counter the answer to the first is trivial, and way 1 is perfectly fine. For anything bigger, such as a state machine (see the next chapter) or a pipeline stage, the next-state logic can be dozens of lines of if and case, and keeping it out of the clocked block makes it far easier to read and to check. The HIPV SoC uses this idea in its 64-bit timer counter, cntr, which computes plus_one = count + 1 with an assign and feeds it to a register cell with an enable and a clear, instead of writing the increment inside the clocked block.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.10 Combinational logic
We now do the same for combinational circuits. The method is identical: hardware, waveform, code, walk through. The difference is in the waveform: there is no clock, because a combinational output depends only on the current inputs, so it changes as soon as an input does.
The block for it is always_comb. It re-evaluates whenever any signal it reads changes. It is closer to a spreadsheet formula that recalculates on every input edit than to a function you call. You write no sensitivity list, since the tool works it out from the signals the block reads. The assignment inside is the blocking =, which reads as “this is what the output equals right now”. There is no state to remember, which gives one rule that matters more than any other: every output must be assigned on every path through the block.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.11 The multiplexer






Figure 5.10: A 2-to-1 multiplexer: Y follows D0 while S is 0 and D1 while S is 1, with no clock.



A multiplexer selects one of several inputs. The 2-to-1 version is the first cell in rtl/generic, and HIPV writes it as a continuous assignment:
module mux2 #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D0, D1,
  input  logic             S,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Y);

  assign Y = S ? D1 : D0;

endmodule
Figure 5.10 shows what it does. There is no clock: Y equals D0 while S is 0 and D1 while S is 1, and it changes the moment the selected input or the select changes. At the start of column 2 D0 rises, and since S is 0, so does Y. At the start of column 3 S rises, Y switches over to D1, which is 0, and falls. At column 4 D1 rises, Y follows. At column 6 S falls and Y returns to D0, which is 1.
The same multiplexer in an always_comb block reads like this:
always_comb begin
  if (S) Y = D1;
  else   Y = D0;
end
Both give the same circuit. The assign form is shorter for one line of logic; the always_comb form is better when there are several outputs or several conditions. For a multiplexer with more than two inputs, the case statement is clearer than a chain of ?: operators. HIPV’s 3-to-1 multiplexer, written with a chain of conditional operators in the repository, looks like this as an always_comb with case:
module mux3 #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
  input  logic [WIDTH-1:0] D0, D1, D2,
  input  logic [1:0]       S,
  output logic [WIDTH-1:0] Y);

  always_comb begin
    case (S)
      2'b01:   Y = D1;
      2'b10:   Y = D2;
      default: Y = D0;    // 2'b00, and 2'b11 falls back to D0
    endcase
  end
endmodule
The case compares S against each listed value and runs the matching branch. The default branch is not optional: it makes sure Y is assigned for every value of S, including the one the designer never intended to use (2'b11), and values containing X or Z in simulation. The synthesized circuit (Figure 5.11) is two comparators and two 2-to-1 multiplexers in series.






Figure 5.11: The mux3 cell as drawn by Yosys from the HIPV file: S == 2'b10 selects D2, otherwise S == 2'b01 selects D1, otherwise D0.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.12 The decoder






Figure 5.12: An address decoder: one SlaveSel bit goes high for each mapped region, and DecErr goes high for an unmapped address.



A decoder turns an encoded value into a set of separate control signals, and it is everywhere in a processor: the instruction decoder turns an opcode into control signals, and the bus decoder turns an address into “which device is being accessed”. The second one is a clean example. The HIPV crossbar has five slaves (instruction memory, data memory, UART, timer and GPIO), each mapped to a region of the address space, and the decoder produces a one-hot select, one bit per slave, plus an error flag for an address that belongs to no slave. Here it is with the address map written out:
module addr_decoder (
    input  logic [31:0] Addr,
    output logic [4:0]  SlaveSel,
    output logic        DecErr
);
  always_comb begin
    SlaveSel = '0;                                     // default: nothing selected
    if (Addr[31:16] == 16'h0000)  SlaveSel[0] = 1'b1;  // instruction memory, 64 KiB
    if (Addr[31:16] == 16'h1000)  SlaveSel[1] = 1'b1;  // data memory, 64 KiB
    if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20000) SlaveSel[2] = 1'b1;  // UART, 4 KiB
    if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20001) SlaveSel[3] = 1'b1;  // timer, 4 KiB
    if (Addr[31:12] == 20'h20002) SlaveSel[4] = 1'b1;  // GPIO, 4 KiB
  end

  assign DecErr = ~|SlaveSel;
endmodule
Read the waveform first (Figure 5.12). Five addresses arrive one after another, two columns each. The first, 0x0000_0040, lies in the instruction-memory region, so SlaveSel[0] goes high. The next addresses hit data memory, the UART and the timer in turn, and each raises exactly one select. The last, 0x3000_0000, matches no region: every select stays low, so DecErr rises. Only one select is ever high, because the regions do not overlap.
Now the code. The first statement in the block is the important one: SlaveSel = '0 assigns the default, every bit low, before anything else. Each if then overrides one bit. Because every bit of SlaveSel has a value on every path, whatever the address, the block cannot build a latch, and none of the ifs needs an else. This default first, then override pattern is the safest way to write always_comb, and you will see it throughout HIPV. The last line uses the reduction operator from the previous chapter: ~|SlaveSel is true when no select bit is set.
(The real obi_decoder in the HIPV repository is the same block, with the base addresses and sizes taken from a shared package, so that adding a slave changes one file.)

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.13 Avoiding latches
The decoder showed the right way. Here is the wrong way:
always_comb begin
  if (sel) y = in1;
end
When sel is 0, no branch assigns y. In a spreadsheet an unhandled case would show a blank cell, but in hardware an output cannot go blank. If no branch assigns it, the only way to keep it at some value is to remember the previous one, so the tool builds a latch, the element from earlier in this chapter (Figure 5.13). It adds a storage element you did not intend, it complicates timing analysis, and it is the most common bug in always_comb. Tools warn about it, which is the reason to use always_comb instead of the old always @(*).






Figure 5.13: What synthesis builds for an incomplete if: a latch whose enable is sel, so y holds its old value whenever sel is 0.



There are three ways to follow the rule. Give every output a default at the top of the block, as the decoder does. Or write an else on every if. Or give every case a default branch, as in mux3. Sequential blocks are different: inside always_ff, a missing assignment simply means “keep the value”, which is what a flip-flop does anyway.

5.18 Running a simulation
Any SystemVerilog simulator can run these testbenches. With the open-source Icarus Verilog, you compile the design together with its testbench and run the result:
iverilog -g2012 -o sim_counter counter4.sv tb_counter.sv
vvp sim_counter
The -g2012 option selects the SystemVerilog language level. To look at waveforms instead of printed lines, add two statements at the start of the initial block, and open the resulting file in GTKWave:
$dumpfile("tb_counter.vcd");
$dumpvars(0, tb_counter);
The waveforms you get are the same kind as the ones drawn in this chapter, and reading them is the same skill. Checking results by eye does not scale beyond a handful of signals, though. A testbench that compares outputs against expected values, as ours does with $error, can be run again after every change and report a clear pass or fail. Later in the course we move this idea to a Python framework, cocotb, which makes writing such checks much easier.

title: 5  Designing with SystemVerilog
text:
5.19 From design to the pipeline
Everything introduced here is the working vocabulary of the rest of the course. always_ff with non-blocking assignment and a synchronous reset is how every pipeline register is built, through flopenr and its siblings. always_comb with a default at the top is how the ALU and the decoders avoid latch inference. Instances and parameters are how those cells are assembled into stages, and stages into a processor. The pipeline chapters introduce no new syntax: they put these constructs to work on a larger example.

title: 6  Finite State Machines
text:
6.2 Theoretical foundations
The first part of this chapter is the theory: what a finite state machine is, the ways to draw one, how it maps onto hardware, and how it is written in SystemVerilog. We use a small example throughout, a controller for window blinds. The second part (Section 6.3) applies all of it to a complete design, a traffic light.

6.2.1 What is a finite state machine?
A finite state machine (FSM) is a model of a system that, at any moment, is in one of a finite number of internal states. The state summarizes everything about the past that matters for the future: the machine does not remember how it got into a state, only which state it is in. At each clock edge, the machine moves to a next state, which depends on the current state and on the external inputs, and it produces outputs that depend on the state and, in some machines, on the inputs as well.
Formally, an FSM is a tuple \((S, I, O, \delta, \lambda, s_0)\):

\(S\) is the finite set of states, and \(s_0 \in S\) the initial state, the one the machine enters on reset;
\(I\) and \(O\) are the sets of input and output values;
\(\delta : S \times I \to S\) is the next-state function, which gives the next state for each combination of current state and input;
\(\lambda\) is the output function.

A counter is the simplest example: its states are the values 0 to 15, its next-state function is “add one”, and it has no inputs apart from the reset. FSMs become interesting when the inputs steer them.
In a digital system, FSMs are the controllers. A larger design is usually split into a datapath, the registers, adders and multiplexers that process the data, and a control path, which examines the external commands and the status of the datapath and activates the right control signals at the right time. A UART transmitter, a bus interface waiting for a response, a memory controller sequencing a read: in each of them, the part that decides what happens next is an FSM.


6.2.2 Describing an FSM: the state diagram






Figure 6.1: State diagram of the window-blinds controller, a Mealy machine: each arrow is labelled with its condition and, after the slash, the outputs that are 1 on that transition.



The most common way to describe an FSM is a state diagram: a directed graph in which every node is a state and every arrow a transition.
Take a controller for window blinds. A single push button controls a servo motor: if the blinds are up, a press pushes them down; if they are down, a press pulls them up. The FSM has one input, Button, and two outputs, Push and Pull, which drive the motor. It must remember where the blinds are, so it needs two states, UP and DOWN (Figure 6.1).
Each arrow is labelled with a condition and, after a slash, the outputs that are 1 when the machine takes that arrow. In UP, if Button is 1 the machine raises Push and moves to DOWN. If Button is 0, it takes the arrow back to UP, and no output is active (the – after the slash). DOWN is the mirror image, with Pull. The arrow marked reset shows the initial state.
Designing an FSM always follows the same three steps, and the state diagram is where they are written down:

Define the states. What must the machine remember? Here, whether the blinds are up or down.
Define the transitions. For each state and each input combination, which state comes next? Every state must have a way out for every input combination, even if that way is “stay here”.
Define the outputs. Which outputs are active, in which state, and under which input?

The same information can be written as a state table, one row per state and input combination:



State
Button
Next state

The table is the next-state function \(\delta\) and the output function \(\lambda\) written out in full. It is the most precise description, but it grows with every state and every input bit, so for anything but tiny machines we draw the diagram instead.


6.2.3 The structure of an FSM in hardware






Figure 6.2: The general structure of an FSM: the next-state logic, the state register, and the output logic of a Moore or a Mealy machine.



In hardware, every FSM has the same three parts (Figure 6.2):

The state register stores the current state. It is a set of flip-flops, all clocked by the system clock, and it is the only memory in the machine. On reset it loads the initial state.
The next-state logic is a combinational circuit that implements \(\delta\): from the current state and the inputs, it computes NextState, which the register loads at the next clock edge.
The output logic is a combinational circuit that implements \(\lambda\) and produces the outputs.

The loop from the register output, through the next-state logic, and back into the register is the same loop as in the counter of the previous chapter, written in its way 2: the register only stores, and all the decisions are in the combinational logic in front of it. An FSM is a counter whose “+ 1” has been replaced by an arbitrary function of the state and the inputs.


6.2.4 Moore and Mealy machines






Figure 6.3: The blinds controller in simulation. Button comes from a synchronous edge detector and is high for one cycle; Push and Pull respond in the same cycle, State at the next edge.



The output logic in Figure 6.2 comes in two forms, and they give the two classic kinds of FSM:

In a Moore machine, the outputs depend only on the current state: \(\lambda : S \to O\). The outputs are written inside the states of the diagram, and they change only at a clock edge, when the state changes. A traffic light is a Moore machine: the lamps are a function of the state.
In a Mealy machine, the outputs depend on the current state and the inputs: \(\lambda : S \times I \to O\). The outputs are written on the arrows, as in Figure 6.1. The blinds controller is a Mealy machine: Push is 1 only in UP and only while Button is 1.

Figure 6.3 shows what this means in time. In column 2 Button is 1, and Push is 1 in that same cycle, before the state has changed; the state becomes DOWN only at the edge that starts column 3. The same happens with Pull in column 6.
The two kinds trade speed against safety:

A Mealy machine reacts one cycle earlier and often needs fewer states. To get a one-cycle Push pulse from a Moore machine, the blinds controller would need extra states such as PUSHING and PULLING, in which the output is active. The price of a Mealy machine is the combinational path from input to output. Any glitch on the input appears on the output, and the path adds to the timing of whatever the output drives. If two Mealy machines feed each other, the paths can even close into a combinational loop. In this book we prefer Moore outputs, and use Mealy outputs where the one-cycle reaction really matters, for example for a one-cycle Done pulse.


6.2.5 State encoding
The states have names in the diagram, but the state register stores bits, so every state needs a binary code. The choice of codes is the state encoding, and there are three common ones. For \(N\) states:

Binary encoding numbers the states 0, 1, 2, … and needs \(\lceil \log_2 N \rceil\) flip-flops. It is the most compact.
Gray encoding uses the same number of flip-flops, but assigns codes so that states that follow each other differ in a single bit. That reduces switching activity, and so power, when the machine mostly moves along a fixed sequence.
One-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, and exactly one of them is 1 at a time. It needs \(N\) flip-flops, but the logic becomes very simple: “are we in GREEN?” is a single bit, not a comparison.

For the four states of the traffic light in the second part of this chapter:

The traffic light cycles RED, RED_YELLOW, GREEN, YELLOW, RED, so with the Gray codes every transition flips exactly one bit, including the one back to the start.
On an FPGA, flip-flops are plentiful (every slice has eight of them, as we saw in the FPGA chapter), while logic depth decides the clock speed. One-hot encoding trades a few flip-flops for shallower next-state and output logic, and is often the fastest choice. In practice, the synthesis tool recognizes FSMs in the code and usually picks the encoding itself: Vivado re-encodes a machine it extracts, and can be overruled with the fsm_encoding attribute. What we write in the code is the meaning of the states, and the encoding is an implementation detail.


6.2.6 The ASM chart






Figure 6.4: ASM chart of the blinds controller. The Mealy outputs Push and Pull appear in conditional output boxes, on the path where Button is 1.



A state diagram gets crowded quickly: when there are several inputs, and when the machine also has to update counters or registers, the labels on the arrows become long expressions. An algorithmic state machine (ASM) chart shows the same information as a flowchart, which is easier to follow step by step. It uses three kinds of boxes (Figure 6.4):

A rectangular state box stands for one state. It holds the state name and the Moore outputs that are 1 in that state. Outputs that are not listed are 0.
A diamond is a decision box. It tests an input or an internal signal, and has a 0 and a 1 exit.
A rounded conditional output box holds the Mealy outputs that are 1 on that path, and the register updates (such as Count++) that happen on that path.

A state box with all the decision and conditional boxes below it, up to the arrows that enter the next state boxes, forms an ASM block, and one ASM block is one clock cycle. During the cycle, the machine is in the state of the state box, the decisions are evaluated by the next-state logic, and the outputs of the conditional boxes on the active path are 1. At the clock edge the machine follows the active path into the next state.
Compare Figure 6.4 with Figure 6.1: the self-loops of the state diagram are the 0 exits of the decisions, and the outputs that were written after the slash are now in the conditional boxes. The ASM chart has another advantage: it maps line by line onto the SystemVerilog code, as the next section shows.


6.2.7 Describing an FSM in SystemVerilog
The three hardware parts of Figure 6.2 become three pieces of code. Here is the blinds controller, written according to the HIPV coding conventions:
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
// blinds_fsm
//
// Purpose: Window-blinds controller. A press of Button pushes the
//          blinds down when they are up, and pulls them up when
//          they are down.
///////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

module blinds_fsm(
  input  logic clk, reset,
  input  logic Button,
  output logic Pull, Push);

  typedef enum logic {UP, DOWN} state_t;

  state_t State, NextState;

  // state register
  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    if (reset) State <= UP;
    else       State <= NextState;

  // next-state logic
  always_comb begin
    NextState = State;                     // default: stay
    case (State)
      UP:      if (Button) NextState = DOWN;
      DOWN:    if (Button) NextState = UP;
      default: NextState = UP;
    endcase
  end

  // output logic (Mealy: depends on the state and the input)
  assign Push = (State == UP) && Button;
  assign Pull = (State == DOWN) && Button;

endmodule
The states are an enumerated type. typedef enum logic {UP, DOWN} state_t; defines a new type, state_t, whose values have names. The simulator shows those names in the waveform instead of bits, and the compiler refuses to assign an unrelated value to a state_t signal without a cast. Without explicit values the encoding is binary, in the order listed; to choose another encoding, give the values explicitly:
typedef enum logic [3:0] {RED        = 4'b0001,     // one-hot
                          RED_YELLOW = 4'b0010,
                          GREEN      = 4'b0100,
                          YELLOW     = 4'b1000} state_t;
Following the HIPV naming convention, the state names are constants and are written in MACRO_CASE, the type name ends in _t, and the signals State and NextState are in UpperCamelCase.
The state register is an always_ff with a synchronous reset, exactly the register of the previous chapter. Reset loads the initial state.
The next-state logic is an always_comb with a case on the current state, one branch per state. It begins by assigning the default NextState = State, “stay where you are”. This is the default first, then override pattern: every if without an else falls back on the default, which is exactly the 0 exit of a decision in the ASM chart, and NextState is assigned on every path, so no latch can appear. The default branch of the case catches state codes that do not belong to any state. With two states in one bit there are none, but in a one-hot machine most of the codes are illegal, and the default sends the machine back to a known state instead of leaving it stuck.
The output logic is two assign statements. Because they read Button, this is a Mealy machine. In a Moore machine, the output logic reads only State.
One practical remark. Button must be a one-cycle pulse that is synchronous to clk. A real push button is neither: it bounces for milliseconds, and it is held for millions of clock cycles, during which this FSM would toggle at every edge. On a board, the button first passes through a synchronizer, a debouncer and an edge detector, and only their one-cycle output reaches the FSM. We return to synchronizers in a later chapter.


6.2.8 FSMs with data registers
The blinds controller remembers one bit. Real controllers also have to remember numbers: how many bits of a UART frame have been sent, or how many milliseconds a traffic light has been green. In principle we could make every count a separate state (GREEN_0, GREEN_1, …, GREEN_3999), but that is absurd. Instead, we keep the counter in a register next to the state register. The state is then the named control state plus the contents of these data registers, and the machine is called an FSM with datapath (FSMD).
The coding pattern stays the same, and extends to every such register. Each register X gets a companion signal XNext:

X is the current value, the output of the register;
XNext is the next value, computed by the next-state logic, and loaded into X at the next clock edge.

The always_ff block loads all of them together (State <= NextState; Count <= CountNext;), and the always_comb block computes all the ...Next signals, each with its default first: CountNext = Count means “keep the value”, and a branch overrides it where the count must change. In an ASM chart, the register updates are the contents of the conditional boxes, written as Count++ or Count = 0. All updates in one ASM block happen at the same clock edge, together with the change of state. The second part of this chapter uses this pattern for the millisecond counter of the traffic light.


6.2.9 Common mistakes
Most FSM bugs fall into a few groups:

Latches. If some path through the next-state logic does not assign NextState (or a ...Next register value), the tool infers a latch. Start the always_comb block with the defaults.
Trap states. A state code that no branch handles can keep the machine stuck forever after a glitch or a bad reset. Give every case a default branch that returns to a known state.
Derived clocks. Slowing an FSM down by clocking it with a counter bit creates a second clock domain and breaks timing analysis. Keep the system clock everywhere, and let the counter produce a one-cycle enable (tick) that the FSM checks, as the traffic light does below.
Asynchronous inputs. An input that can change at any moment, such as a button or a serial line, can violate the setup time of the state register and leave the FSM in an illegal state. Pass it through a synchronizer first.
Mealy chains. A Mealy output that feeds the input of another Mealy machine, whose output comes back, forms a combinational loop. Register one of the outputs, or use Moore outputs.

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.1 Goal for this week

Place the HIPV SoC on the levels of abstraction, from the system down to the silicon, and know at which level we design
Translate the well-known pipeline theory (IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB) into SystemVerilog
Apply SystemVerilog syntax immediately on a real, motivating example
Treat memory (for now) as an interface — the implementation follows next week

We implement pipeline registers as separate modules for two reasons. First, pedagogically: each such register is a direct, visible example of a D flip-flop (DFF) in the context of a real processor, which was an explicit goal of the second part of the course. Second, practically: separate modules with a fixed interface (see pipeline_pkg.sv) allow us to substitute an individual stage with a reference (“golden”) implementation in the jigsaw testing methodology — discussed in more detail in the verification chapter. This five-stage IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB structure follows the classic pipelined datapath described by Patterson and Hennessy (2017).

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.2 Levels of abstraction






Figure 7.1: The HIPV SoC at six levels of abstraction. We design at the register-transfer level; the tools, the FPGA vendor and the foundry take care of the levels below.



Before we build the pipeline, it helps to step back and look at what we are building from a distance. The HIPV SoC is a single system, but it can be described at very different levels of detail: as a handful of blocks connected by buses, as an algorithm that executes instructions, as a set of registers and the logic between them, as a netlist of gates, as a circuit of transistors, or as structures in doped silicon. These are the levels of abstraction of digital design (Figure 7.1).
Each level describes the same system, but with fewer details than the level below it. A description at a higher level is shorter and easier to reason about, because it hides how its parts are built: at the system level the core is a box, and we do not care whether its adder is a ripple-carry chain or a carry-lookahead tree. A description at a lower level is closer to the real hardware, and much larger. Moving down a level means adding implementation decisions; moving up means leaving them out.
The earlier chapters of this book have already visited most of these levels, bottom-up: silicon and the p-n junction, CMOS transistors and gates, programmable devices and the FPGA, and finally SystemVerilog at the register-transfer level. In this chapter we start working top-down, the way a design is actually made, and we use HIPV as the example at every level.

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.4 Algorithmic level
At the algorithmic level, a block is described by what it computes, as an algorithm, without any notion of a clock or of the hardware that will carry it out. For the HIPV core, that algorithm is the RV32I instruction set: a loop that fetches the instruction at the program counter, decodes it, and executes it:
PC = 0
forever:
  instr = mem[PC]                               # fetch
  op, rd, rs1, rs2, imm = decode(instr)         # decode
  a = x[rs1];  b = x[rs2]
  case op:                                      # execute, memory, write back
    ALU:    x[rd] = alu(op, a, b or imm);  PC = PC + 4
    LOAD:   x[rd] = mem[a + imm];          PC = PC + 4
    STORE:  mem[a + imm] = b;              PC = PC + 4
    BRANCH: PC = taken(op, a, b) ? PC + imm : PC + 4
    JAL:    x[rd] = PC + 4;                PC = PC + imm
    JALR:   x[rd] = PC + 4;                PC = (a + imm) & ~1
Here x is the array of 32 registers (with x[0] always 0) and mem is the memory. Every instruction is finished before the next one starts, and how long each step takes is not part of the description. This is the level of the RISC-V specification, and of an instruction-set simulator such as Spike, which runs programs exactly according to this loop. It is the reference against which every implementation is judged: whatever the pipeline does internally, the registers and the memory must end up as the loop says.

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.5 Register-transfer level






Figure 7.2: The HIPV core at the register-transfer level: five pipeline stages with their handshakes, the redirect and write-back feedback, the two OBI ports and the hazard unit.



At the register-transfer level (RTL), the algorithm is mapped onto clocked hardware: a set of registers, and the combinational logic that computes their next values at every clock edge. This is where time appears. The loop of the algorithmic level is cut into five steps, fetch, decode, execute, memory and write back, and each step becomes a pipeline stage with its own registers, so that five instructions can be in progress at once (Figure 7.2). The price is that instructions now overlap, and the RTL must handle what the algorithm never had to think about: an instruction that needs a result its predecessor has not yet written (forwarding, in the hazard unit), and instructions fetched after a jump that must be thrown away (the redirect from Execute).
This is the level of hipv_core.sv and of everything we have written in SystemVerilog so far: the leaf cells (flopenr, mux2, mux3, adder) in behavioral style, the stages assembled from them structurally, and the control FSMs. It is the lowest level at which we still make the design decisions ourselves, and the highest level that tools can turn into hardware automatically. That is why almost all digital design is done here, and why the rest of this course works at this level.

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.7 Transistor level
At the transistor level, each cell is a circuit of NMOS and PMOS transistors, the CMOS circuits from the first chapters. On an FPGA, the transistor-level design is fixed and was done once, by the vendor, for the whole family. A LUT6 is 64 SRAM cells that hold its truth table, followed by a tree of pass-transistor multiplexers selected by the six inputs. Every programmable routing switch is a pass transistor controlled by another SRAM cell. Flip-flops and the carry chain are hard-wired CMOS circuits. Our HIPV design does not change a single transistor: it only sets the configuration cells that decide what the existing transistors do.
For an ASIC, this level is where the standard cells come from: each cell of the library is designed and characterized once at the transistor level, and synthesis then uses it as a black box with known delay and power.

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.8 Material level
At the bottom, at the material level, a transistor is a physical structure: regions of n-type and p-type silicon created by doping, a thin oxide, a polysilicon or metal gate, and layers of metal wiring on top, produced by photolithography. The behavior of the p-n junction and of the MOSFET channel, described in the first chapter, is determined here. The Artix-7 xc7a100t on our board is manufactured in a 28 nm process, and the layout and process decisions at this level belong to the foundry and to the FPGA vendor.

title: 7  Five-Stage Pipeline — Structure
text:
7.9 Moving between the levels
A design is made top-down. We start at the system level (which blocks, which bus), specify the behavior at the algorithmic level (the RV32I instruction set), and write the RTL by hand. From there on, the tools take over: synthesis produces the gate-level netlist, and place and route maps it onto the transistors and wires of the FPGA, which the vendor and the foundry designed at the two lowest levels.
Verification connects the levels in the opposite direction. We simulate the RTL and compare its results with what the higher level says must happen: the HIPV core testbenches run small programs and check that the data memory ends up exactly as the algorithmic loop above predicts. Each level is thus both the specification for the level below and the reference for checking it.




Patterson, David A., and John L. Hennessy. 2017. Computer Organization and Design RISC-v Edition: The Hardware Software Interface. Morgan Kaufmann.

title: 8  Instruction fetch unit
8  Instruction fetch unit
text:
8.3 Interface of the IFU
The ports of the IFU fall into four groups: the handshake with the Decode stage, the redirect from the Execute stage, the stage outputs, and the port to the instruction memory. The suffix of every name says which stage the signal belongs to: F for Fetch, D for Decode, E for Execute.
module ifu (input  logic        clk, reset,
            // pipeline handshake and redirect
            input  logic        ReadyD,
            output logic        ValidF,
            input  logic        PCSrcE,
            input  logic [31:0] PCTargetE,
            // stage outputs to Decode
            output logic [31:0] InstrF,
            output logic [31:0] PCF, PCPlus4F,
            // OBI master port to instruction memory
            output logic        ObiReqF,
            input  logic        ObiGntF,
            output logic [31:0] ObiAddrF,
            input  logic        ObiRvalidF,
            input  logic [31:0] ObiRdataF);

8.3.1 Handshake with Decode






Figure 8.1: The handshake between the IFU and Decode. InstrF holds I0 from cycle 4 to 9, but it is a valid instruction only while ValidF is high. Decode is busy in cycles 4 and 5 (ReadyD = 0), so I0 waits; it is transferred at the end of cycle 6, where both signals are high.



The IFU and Decode work at their own pace, so they agree on each transfer with two signals:

ValidF (output) says that the output of the IFU is valid: the bits on InstrF are a fetched instruction, not leftovers from an earlier one or random bits after reset.
ReadyD (input) says that Decode is ready to accept a new instruction.

An instruction moves from Fetch to Decode at a clock edge where both signals are high. While ValidF is high and ReadyD is low, the IFU keeps its outputs stable and waits. Figure 8.1 shows both cases. Note that InstrF itself does not tell whether it is valid: between cycles 7 and 9 it still holds I0, which has already been handed over, and only ValidF = 0 tells Decode to ignore it. The same pair of signals connects every two neighbouring stages of HIPV, which is why the pipeline is called elastic: a slow stage simply holds back the stages in front of it.


8.3.2 Redirect from Execute
Jumps and branches are resolved in the Execute stage, and Execute tells the IFU about them with two signals:

PCSrcE is one bit: 1 means that a jump or a taken branch has occurred, so the next PC is the target; 0 means normal, sequential execution.
PCTargetE is the 32-bit target address.

PCSrcE lasts exactly one clock cycle. In HIPV it is ValidEReg & ReadyM & (JumpE | JalrE | (BranchE & TakenE)): it is high only in the cycle in which the branch leaves Execute. In that same cycle the instruction in Decode is flushed (its valid bit is gated with ~PCSrcE), so in the next cycle Execute holds a bubble and PCSrcE drops back to 0. The IFU must therefore react to the redirect in the cycle it sees it. It cannot look at PCSrcE again later, which is the root of the discard flag (Section 8.5.2).


8.3.3 Stage outputs
The IFU hands three values to Decode:

InstrF, the fetched instruction;
PCF, the address the instruction was fetched from;
PCPlus4F, the address of the next instruction, PCF + 4.

The two PC values are not needed in the IFU, but in later stages. Execute adds an offset to PCF to compute the target of a branch or of jal, and auipc adds an immediate to it. PCPlus4F is the return address that jal and jalr write into the destination register. Both travel down the pipeline together with their instruction.


8.3.4 Port to instruction memory






Figure 8.2: Two read transactions on the OBI port. In the address phase (cycles 1–2, 5–6) ObiReqF and ObiAddrF are held until the memory grants the request with ObiGntF. In the response phase, at least one cycle later, ObiRvalidF marks the cycle in which ObiRdataF carries the instruction.



The IFU reads instructions over the OBI (Open Bus Interface) protocol, which we discuss in detail later in the semester. For now, a simplified view is enough. The IFU only reads, so it uses five signals:








Signal
Direction
Meaning




ObiReqF
out
request: the IFU wants to start a read


ObiAddrF
out
address of the location to read


ObiGntF
in
grant: the memory has accepted the request


ObiRvalidF
in
response valid: ObiRdataF carries the read data


ObiRdataF
in
the data read, here an instruction



Each read, or transaction, has two phases (Figure 8.2). In the address phase, the IFU raises ObiReqF and puts the address on ObiAddrF, and keeps both until the memory answers with ObiGntF. At the edge where ObiReqF and ObiGntF are both high, the memory has taken the address. This is the same valid/ready idea as the handshake with Decode. In the response phase, at least one cycle after the grant, the memory raises ObiRvalidF for one cycle, and in that cycle ObiRdataF holds the instruction. Outside that cycle, ObiRdataF is meaningless.
The memory decides how long each phase takes. In Figure 8.2 it grants after one wait cycle and responds one cycle after the grant, but a slower memory may need more cycles for either. Two properties are important for the controller. First, once the request is granted, the response will come, and the protocol has no way of cancelling it. Second, a response carries no tag that says which request it belongs to: responses come back in the order of the requests. HIPV keeps at most one transaction in flight at a time, so the response always belongs to the last granted request.

title: 8  Instruction fetch unit

8  Instruction fetch unit
text:
8.6 Summary
The IFU is a small datapath, the PC loop and the instruction register, built from the generic blocks flopenr, mux2 and adder, and a controller that decides when each of them acts. The controller is a three-state FSM with one extra bit of memory, the discard flag, which remembers a jump for as long as a stale instruction is on its way from memory.
The design makes two deliberate simplifications. It keeps one memory transaction in flight at a time, which limits it to one instruction every three cycles. And a jump in REQUEST, before the grant, changes ObiAddrF while ObiReqF is high. Strict OBI requires the address to stay stable during the address phase, but simple memories, which take the address only in the cycle of the grant, tolerate the change. Both are natural extensions for later in the course.
